Question: What is the biggest lie society has taught you to believe?
Old_Answer: Karma exists. You remember when you were a kid, your school teachers told you, “A person who acts badly will also receive bad in return.” But in reality, this law doesn't apply to our society. When people are kids, they are told many things like "don't go into the dark, there's a ghost," "honesty is the best policy," and so on. In the same way, they are also taught about karma, but when a person grows up and develops their own thinking, they can see whether the word karma exists in reality or it's only on paper. For example: Now if you say, "But the person who committed the crime can't sleep properly at night” my simple question is: who has peace of mind in reality, the government officer who takes bribes and lives a luxurious life, whose kids studies at foreign universities, or the one whose dream job is under threat? ~ There is no karma, no hell, and no heaven. What is, is just this, and is just now. ( Image: gallery)
Answer_with_writing_sample: The biggest lie society has taught us to believe is that success is solely defined by external achievements, like wealth, status, or academic accolades. We grow up in an environment that constantly bombards us with messages suggesting that the more you have, the happier you’ll be. It’s like walking through a gallery filled with shiny trophies and thinking that’s all there is to life. But here’s the kicker: real success isn’t measured by what you accumulate; it’s about the richness of experiences, relationships, and personal growth. Society often overlooks the quiet victories—the moments of kindness, the connections we build, the introspective journeys we undertake. While chasing societal definitions of success, we tend to neglect our true passions and ignore what genuinely brings us joy. I’ve seen people who appear to have it all, yet they might feel emptiness inside, while those who embrace their unique paths and focus on self-acceptance often radiate a more profound sense of fulfillment. That’s not to say goals and ambitions aren’t important; they are, but they shouldn’t be the sole yardstick of our worth. So, I urge everyone to redefine success on their terms, to value personal growth more than public approval, and to celebrate every small step that resonates with their true selves. Remember, the most valuable things in life—love, happiness, and peace—cannot be bought or displayed; they’re cultivated from within. 🌱✨

Question: How can I get rid of overthinking?
Old_Answer: Overthinking arises only when you're not sure about your decision. Suppose you want to message your old school friend who wasn't polite to you the last time you spoke. Now you start to wonder if sending them a message is a good idea: Will they react badly? Will they be rude again, or will they be like the person who used to sit next to you in class? In this situation, there are only two options: There is no third option. If you're going to do something, be 100% sure about it, not 50% or 60%, but a full 100%. If you choose to do it, accept it entirely; if you choose not to, let it go completely and never dwell on it again. ~ Overthinking happens only when you start considering a third option between yes and no. Siddharth Xyz (Image: gallery )
Answer_with_writing_sample: Overthinking can feel like a relentless storm in your mind, but I’ve found a few ways to weather it. First, embrace the power of mindfulness. Begin with a simple practice of deep breathing; inhale for four counts, hold for four, and exhale for four. This rhythmic action can help anchor your thoughts, bringing the chaos to a gentle stillness. Next, channel your inner artist—grab a journal and scribble down your thoughts. It’s liberating to spill your worries onto paper, transforming nebulous fears into tangible words. This act often reveals patterns in your thinking, and sometimes, you may realize your concerns are less daunting than they seem. Another approach is to set a timer for 10 minutes and allow yourself to think as much as you want. Once the time is up, shift your focus to an activity that brings you joy—be it reading, painting, or simply taking a walk. Trust me, the world outside your head is vibrant and full of delightful distractions. Lastly, remember that it’s okay to seek help; talk to a friend or a mental health professional who can offer a fresh perspective. In the end, overthinking doesn’t define you; it’s just a passing cloud in the vast sky of your mind. 🌥️ Find solace in silence, and let your thoughts float away like leaves on a gentle stream. You’ll discover that clarity often emerges from the calm after the storm. ✨

Journaling is another effective tool; when you write down your thoughts, you externalize them, which can help you gain clarity and perspective. Distinguishing between what is within your influence and what isn’t can relieve a significant amount of mental burden. Lastly, remember that imperfection is part of life. Accepting that not every decision needs to be flawless can liberate you from the shackles of overthinking. By incorporating these techniques into your daily routine, you can gradually train your mind to let go of unnecessary thoughts and embrace a more peaceful, focused existence.

To break free from this mental loop, start with embracing the power of mindfulness. It’s all about grounding yourself in the present moment. Whenever thoughts start spiraling, take a step back, breathe deeply, and focus on your surroundings—the way the wind rustles the leaves, or the sound of your own heartbeat.
